knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

In this project, we will estimate a phylogenetic tree containing all representative sequences, reference sequences and the outgroup, and root the tree using the outgroup, as well as plot it with clear, informative tip labels.Furthermore, we will use the phylogeny to investigate the taxonomic identity of each sequence group, relate our findings to the food outlets from which the sequences were collected, discuss the strength of the evidence supporting our conclusions, and include any limitations or uncertainties in your analysis.


## 1. Loading the required packages

For this project, we will use the treesurgeon package to calculate the pairwise distances between the sequences and to built the phylogenetic tree based on the distances. Also, we will the msa ,Biostrings, and phangorn packages to read, process, and write data.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(treesurgeon)
library(msa)
library(Biostrings)
library(phangorn)
library(ggplot2)
library(cluster)
```

## 2. Loading and inspecting the data

We have obtained the data of protein alignments from Multiple Sequence Alignment, and we will use it to build the phylogenetic trees and perform further analysis.

```{r}
# load alignments
bacteria_alignment <- readRDS("../Multiple Sequences Alignment/bacteria_alignment.rds")
bacteria_alignment
```

```{r}
# inspect data
image(
  bacteria_alignment, 
  show.labels = TRUE,
  show.nucs = FALSE,
  cex = 0.4,
  col = c(hcl.colors(n = 4, palette = "zissou"), "grey", "white")
)

```

## 3. Calculating pairwise sequence distances

In this part, we will use the JTT to calculate the pairwise protein sequence distances to account for substitutions that are not directly observed.

```{r}
# convert aligned protein sequences to phyDat format
protein <- phyDat(
  as.matrix(bacteria_alignment),
  type = "AA"
)

# calculate JTT-corrected pairwise distances
jtt_distance <- dist.ml(
  protein,
  model = "JTT"
)

# inspect the distance matrix
as.matrix(jtt_distance)[1:3, 1:3]
```

## 4. Estimating a tree from sequence distances

Phylogenetic trees can be estimated using different approaches. Distance-based methods summarise the differences between sequences as pairwise distances and use these distances to estimate a tree. One widely used method is neighbour joining (NJ), a fast algorithm that builds a tree step by step. At each step, it joins the pair of sequences (or clusters) that best satisfies a criterion based on their distances from one another and from all other sequences. It then updates the distances between the resulting clusters and repeats the process until the tree is complete.

```{r}
# Estimate a neighbour-joining tree
nj_tree <- nj(jtt_distance)

# Plot the tree
plot(nj_tree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE, type="unrooted", lab4ut="axial")
```

## 5. Rooting a phylogenetic tree

The neighbour-joining tree is initially unrooted. An unrooted tree represents relationships among sequences but does not indicate the direction of evolution or identify the common ancestor of all the sampled sequences.

If we want to unserstand the order in which lineages diverged, we need to root the tree. One way to do this is to use an outgroup: a sequence or group of sequences known to fall outside the group of primary interest. In our dataset, WP_005894921.1 MULTISPECIES: DNA-directed RNA polymerase subunit beta [Fusobacterium] acts as the outgroup to the mystery bacteria sequences. We can use this sequence to place the root on the branch separating the outgroup from the remaining sequences.

```{r}
# outgroup
OG <- which(nj_tree$tip.label == "WP_005894921.1 MULTISPECIES: DNA-directed RNA polymerase subunit beta [Fusobacterium]")
# Root the tree using the outgroup
rooted_NJtree <- root_node(nj_tree, OG)

# Plot the rooted tree
plot(rooted_NJtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE)
```

By default, trees are plotted with edge.lengths, which represent the estimated nucleotide substitutions per site. This type of tree is called a phylogram. However, when sequences are very closely related, branch lengths can be extremely short, making the branching pattern difficult to see. We can make the relationships easier to visualise by ignoring branch lengths and displaying only the branching pattern. This type of tree is called a cladogram.

```{r}
plot(rooted_NJtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE, use.edge.length = F, x.lim = c(0, 60))

#Each tip is given a unique index from 1-, where Ntip(tree). We can show the tip indexes as follows:
tiplabels(cex = 0.5, adj = c(0, 2))

#Similarly, each internal node is given a unique index from (Ntip(tree)+1) - (Ntip(tree)+Nnode(tree)). We can show the internal node indexes as follows: 
nodelabels(cex = 0.5)
```
The closest relatives of our representative sequences:

outlet_08_seq092 - Lactiplantibacillus plantarum
outlet_01_seq068 - Staphylococcus aureus
outlet_02_seq053 - Bifidobacterium longum and Bifidobacterium sp.
outlet_05_seq074 - Brachybacterium alimentarium
outlet_05_seq033 - Micrococcus luteus

## 6. Estimating a tree using Maximum Likelihood

Neighbor joining (NJ) estimates a phylogenetic tree from pairwise distances between sequences. These distances summarise the differences between each pair of sequences, but they do not explicitly represent the patterns of amino acide changes across the alignment. As a result, the tree that best fits the pairwise distances is not necessarily the tree that best explains the observed sequence data.

An alternative approach is maximum likelihood (ML). Rather than estimating a tree from pairwise distances, ML calculates the probability of the observed alignment given a proposed tree and a model of sequence evolution. It searches for the tree and branch lengths that maximise this likelihood.

ML offers several advantages over NJ. As we have seen, distances between distantly related sequences are noisy, because multiple substitutions at the same site (saturation) make the correction highly uncertain. NJ treats every distance as equally reliable. ML down-weights this unreliable information implicitly: at saturated sites the observed nucleotides are almost equally probable under any tree, so those sites contribute little to distinguishing between trees. ML also assigns a likelihood score to every candidate tree, which allows support for relationships to be evaluated explicitly and alternative models to be compared statistically.

```{r}
# calculate the likelihood of the neighbour-joining tree
fit <- pml(nj_tree, data = protein, model = "JTT")
```

To find a tree with a higher likelihood, we need to optimise the tree’s branch lengths and topology.

```{r}
# Optimise the tree using maximum likelihood
fitJTT <- optim.pml(
  fit,
  rearrangement = "NNI"
)

# Root the maximum-likelihood tree using the outgroup
rooted_JTTtree <- root_node(fitJTT$tree, OG)

# Plot the rooted tree
plot(rooted_JTTtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE)
```

We can visualise the difference between the NJ_tree and the ML_tree using the phytools::cophylo() function:

```{r}
t1 <- rooted_NJtree
t2 <- rooted_JTTtree
t1$edge.length <- NULL
t2$edge.length <- NULL
obj<- cophylo(t1, t2)

plot(obj,link.type="curved",link.lwd=3,link.lty="solid",
     link.col=make.transparent("blue",0.25),fsize=0.3, use.edge.lengths = F)
```

## 7. Assessing support for the tree using bootstrapping

A phylogenetic tree is an estimate of evolutionary relationships, and some branches may be better supported by the data than others. Bootstrap resampling provides a way to assess how consistently the data support the inferred relationships.

In bootstrap resampling, we repeatedly create new datasets by randomly sampling alignment columns with replacement. Each resampled dataset contains the same number of columns as the original alignment, but some sites may appear more than once while others are omitted. We then estimate a phylogenetic tree from each resampled dataset.

We can count how often each edge appears across the resulting trees. This frequency is expressed as a bootstrap support value, usually as a percentage. For example, a support value of 95% means that the corresponding edge was recovered in 95% of the bootstrap trees.

```{r}
#Get bootstrap replicates
bs <- bootstrap.pml(fitJTT, bs=100, multicore = T, optNni=TRUE, control = pml.control(trace = 0))

#get bootstrap support
rooted_JTTtree <- clade_support(trees = bs, con = rooted_JTTtree, digits = 2)

#Plot tree and support values
plot(rooted_JTTtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE, use.edge.length = F)
nodelabels(text = rooted_JTTtree$node.label, col = "darkred", cex = 0.6, frame = "none")
```

## 8. Beyond the JTT model

The Le–Gascuel (LG) model uses a different substitution matrix estimated from a larger and more diverse dataset than JTT model.

```{r}
# Calculate the likelihood of the neighbour-joining tree
fit.1 <- pml(nj_tree, data = protein, model = "LG")

# Optimise the tree using maximum likelihood
fitLG <- optim.pml(
  fit.1,
  rearrangement = "NNI",
  model="LG"
)
```
```{r}
# Root the maximum-likelihood tree using the outgroup
rooted_LGtree <- root_node(fitLG$tree, OG)

# Plot the rooted tree
plot(rooted_LGtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE)
```

## 9. Model selection using AIC

AIC is interpreted comparatively: lower AIC values indicate a preferred model among those being compared. The difference in AIC between two models indicates the relative strength of support for one over the other, with larger differences generally providing stronger evidence in favour of the model with the lower AIC.

```{r}
#Compute difference in AIC between models
AIC(fitJTT) - AIC(fitLG)
```
The LG model is much better supported than JTT: its AIC is approximately 145 units lower, a difference far exceeding the conventional threshold of 10 for substantial support. AIC therefore strongly favours LG over JTT, indicating that its additional parameters improve the fit well beyond what would be expected from added complexity alone.

## 10. Estimating the support for the edges in the LG tree and plot the result

```{r}
#Get bootstrap replicates
bs <- bootstrap.pml(fitLG, bs=100, multicore = T, optNni=TRUE, control = pml.control(trace = 0))

#get bootstrap support
rooted_LGtree <- clade_support(trees = bs, con = rooted_LGtree, digits = 2)

#Plot tree and support values
plot(rooted_LGtree, cex = 0.6, no.margin = TRUE, use.edge.length = F)
nodelabels(text = paste0(
    seq_len(rooted_LGtree$Nnode) + Ntip(rooted_LGtree),
    "-",
    rooted_LGtree$node.label
  ), col = "darkred", cex = 0.6, frame = "none")
```

## 11. Interpreting the phylogenetic tree

The closest relatives to our representative sequences in the inferred phylogenetic tree are as follows:

outlet_08_seq092 - Lactiplantibacillus plantarum
outlet_01_seq068 - Staphylococcus sp. FSL W8-0056
outlet_02_seq053 - Bifidobacterium longum
outlet_05_seq074 - Brachybacterium alimentarium
outlet_05_seq033 - Micrococcus luteus

Bootstrap support describes the reliability of particular clades. We will examine the bootstrap support values of clades related to the relationships between representative sequences and their genetically closest reference sequences.

```{r}
## report bootstrap support values
groups <- c(3, 4, 2, 5, 1)
representatives <- c(
  "outlet_08_seq092",
  "outlet_01_seq068",
  "outlet_02_seq053",
  "outlet_05_seq074",
  "outlet_05_seq033"
)
nodes <- c(50, 43, 41, 37, 31)

# extract bootstrap support from the tree
BS <- as.numeric(
  rooted_LGtree$node.label[
    nodes - Ntip(rooted_LGtree)
  ]
)

# create a summary table
BS_summary <- data.frame(
  Groups = groups,
  Representative = representatives,
  Node = nodes,
  Bootstrap_support = BS,
  BS_percentage = paste0(round(BS * 100), "%")
) 
BS_summary <- BS_summary[order(BS_summary$Groups), ]

BS_summary

```


The inferred phylogenetic tree showed different levels of statistical support. The selected clades containing representatives from groups 1, 4 and 5, associated with the genera Micrococcus, Staphylococcus and Brachybacterium, received strong bootstrap support (100%). However, the relationship between group 2 and Bifidobacterium longum as well as group 3 and Lactiplantibacillus plantarum received lower support (43% and 63%, respectively). In contrast, the broader clades containing the Bifidobacterium and Lactiplantibacillus sequences, including representatives from groups 2 and 3 respectively, both received 100% bootstrap support, strongly supporting the relationships between the two group and the corresponding whole genera, not the species or strains.

Therefore, it can be inferred that sequences from group 1 are likely to be in Micrococcus group, sequences from group 2 are likely to be in Bifidobacterium group, sequences from group 3 are likely to be in Lactiplantibacillus group, sequences from group 4 are likely to be in Staphylococcus group, and sequences from group 5 are likely to be in Brachybacterium group.

## 12. Relating findings to the food outlets

First, we will polt the clusters coloured by outlet:
```{r}
## loading and inspecting data
sequences <- readDNAStringSet("../Data preparation/all_sequences.fasta")
sequences

## aligning the sequences
bacteria_alignment <- msa(sequences, method = "ClustalW", order = "input")
aligned_dna <- msaConvert(
  bacteria_alignment,
  type = "ape::DNAbin"
)

## calculating JC distance
jc.distances <- dist.dna(
  aligned_dna,
  model = "JC69"
)

## performing PCoA
pcoa_result <- cmdscale(
  jc.distances,
  k = 10,
  eig = TRUE
)

pcoa_df <- as.data.frame(pcoa_result$points)
colnames(pcoa_df) <- paste0("PCoA", seq_len(ncol(pcoa_df)))
eig <- pcoa_result$eig
variance <- 100 * eig / sum(eig[eig > 0])

## applying k-means clustering
pcoa_coords <- pcoa_df[, paste0("PCoA", 1:10)]
pcoa_dist <- dist(pcoa_coords)

k_values <- 2:7
mean_silhouette <- numeric(length(k_values))

for (i in seq_along(k_values)) {

  km_test <- kmeans(
    pcoa_coords,
    centers = k_values[i],
    nstart = 25
  )

  sil <- silhouette(km_test$cluster, pcoa_dist)

  mean_silhouette[i] <- mean(sil[, "sil_width"])
}

optimal_k <- k_values[which.max(mean_silhouette)]
set.seed(123)

km_optimal <- kmeans(
  pcoa_coords,
  centers = optimal_k,
  nstart = 25
)
pcoa_df$Clusters <- factor(km_optimal$cluster)
pcoa_df$Sequence <- rownames(pcoa_df)
pcoa_df$outlets <- sub(
  "_seq.*", "",
  pcoa_df$Sequence
)

ggplot(pcoa_df, aes(x = PCoA1, y = PCoA2, colour = outlets)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = paste0("PCoA1 (", round(variance[1], 1), "%)"),
    y = paste0("PCoA2 (", round(variance[2], 1), "%)"),
    title = "K-means Clustering of Bacteria Meat",
    colour = "colour = Food outlets"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

Next, we will inspect the relationship between outlets and clusters:
```{r}
table(pcoa_df$outlets, pcoa_df$Clusters)
```
The findings are as follows:

1. Group 4 (Staphylococcus) only contains sequences collected from food outlets sample 1 and 2, with 9 and 8 sequences respectively, suggesting that Staphylococcus were detected exclusively in these two outlets within this batch of meat. In contrast, group 3 and 5 contain sequences collected from all of food outlets, suggesting that Lactiplantibacillus- and Brachybacterium-associated groups were detected in all of outlets. Similarly, group 1 (Micrococcus) and 2 (Bifidobacterium) were detected in most of outlets;
2. Food outlet 1 contains sequences associated with Micrococcus, Lactiplantibacillus, Staphylococcus, and Brachybacterium. The Staphylococcus-associated group is predominant (9 of 15 sequences), while no sequences belonging to the Bifidobacterium-associated group were detected;
3. Food outlet 2 contains sequences from all five kinds of bacteria, mostly Bifidobacterium and Staphylococcus;
4. Food outlet 3 contains sequences associated with Micrococcus, Lactiplantibacillus, and Brachybacterium. The Micrococcus-associated group is predominant (6 sequences), followed by Brachybacterium (4 sequences). No sequences belonging to the Bifidobacterium- or Staphylococcus-associated groups were detected;
5. Food outlet 4, 5, 6, and 8 contain sequences associated with Micrococcus, Bifidobacterium, Lactiplantibacillus, and Brachybacterium, while their relative abundances varies. No sequences belonging to the Staphylococcus-associated group were detected;
6. Food outlet 7 contains sequences associated with Bifidobacterium, Lactiplantibacillus, and Brachybacterium, with almost even abundance. No sequences belonging to the Micrococcus- or Staphylococcus-associated groups were detected.

Overall, the distribution of bacterial groups varied among the eight food outlets. The Staphylococcus-associated group showed the most restricted distribution, while the Lactiplantibacillus- and Brachybacterium-associated groups were widely distributed.
